claim: Saci1262 transfers a single GlcNAc residue onto a GlcNAc pyrophosphate-linked acceptor molecule.
source: Saci1262 transfers a single GlcNAc residue onto a GlcNAc pyrophosphate-linked acceptor molecule

claim: The MALDI-MS spectra confirmed that Saci1262 transfers a single GlcNAc to both acceptor substrates when incubated with UDP-GlcNAc.
source: The MALDI-MS spectra obtained confirmed that Saci1262 transfers a single GlcNAc to both acceptor substrates when incubated with UDP-GlcNAc (Figure 3B and D).

claim: The Saci1262 assay revealed a shift of the peaks by 203 Da to m/z = 811 [M-1H + 2Na]+ and m/z = 833 [M-2H + 3Na]+, which corresponded to the addition of one dehydrated GlcNAc (203 Da).

claim: Saci1262 does not use UDP-glucose as the sugar donor.

claim: Saci1262 uses exclusively UDP-GlcNAc as the sugar donor.
source: We also investigated Saci1262 promiscuity toward utilizing UDP-glucose as the sugar donor, but no mass shift was observed (Figure 3E), indicating that Saci1262 uses exclusively UDP-GlcNAc.

claim: Based on the confirmed function of Saci1262 as a GT, the protein was named as archaeal glycosylation enzyme 24 (Agl24), in agreement with the general naming procedure of N-glycosylation pathway components in Archaea.
source: Based on the confirmed function of Saci1262 as a GT, we named the protein as archaeal glycosylation enzyme 24 (Agl24), in agreement with the general naming procedure of N-glycosylation pathway components in Archaea (Eichler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a naming decision based on functional characterization and established nomenclature conventions.

claim: S. acidocaldarius is a thermophilic microorganism, with an optimal growth temperature of 75°C.
source: Since S. acidocaldarius is a thermophilic microorganism, with an optimal growth temperature of 75°C (Brock et al., 1972), the temperature dependency of the Agl24 activity was investigated using our established mass spectrometry assay.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Highest activity of Agl24 was detected at 70°C, close to the optimal growth temperature of S. acidocaldarius.
source: Highest activity was detected at 70°C, close to the optimal growth temperature of S. acidocaldarius.
evidence: This is supported by temperature-dependent activity assays.

claim: The addition of EDTA did not affect the activity of Agl24, demonstrating that Agl24 is a metal-independent GT.
source: Furthermore, the addition of EDTA did not affect the activity of Agl24, demonstrating that Agl24 is a metal-independent GT (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by activity assays with EDTA shown in the figures.

claim: The result that Agl24 is metal-independent agrees with the lack of a conserved Asp-X-Asp (DxD) motif in the Agl24 sequence.
source: This result agrees with the lack of a conserved Asp-X-Asp (DxD) motif in the Agl24 sequence, which has been shown to be important to coordinate the metal ions in A-fold GTs, whereas GT-B GTs are metal ion-independent (Lairson et al., 2008; Gloster, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis and known properties of GT-B enzymes, supported by citations.

claim: The conserved Asp-X-Asp (DxD) motif has been shown to be important to coordinate the metal ions in A-fold GTs.
source: This result agrees with the lack of a conserved Asp-X-Asp (DxD) motif in the Agl24 sequence, which has been shown to be important to coordinate the metal ions in A-fold GTs, whereas GT-B GTs are metal ion-independent (Lairson et al., 2008; Gloster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GT-B GTs are metal ion-independent.
source: This result agrees with the lack of a conserved Asp-X-Asp (DxD) motif in the Agl24 sequence, which has been shown to be important to coordinate the metal ions in A-fold GTs, whereas GT-B GTs are metal ion-independent (Lairson et al., 2008; Gloster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The H14A mutant of Agl24 was inactive.
source: The product where the H14 histidine within the conserved GGH14 motif, found in all Alg14 (GSGGH), MurG (GGxGGH), and Agl24 (GGH) homologs, was replaced by an alanine, was inactive (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by activity assays shown in the figure.

claim: The conserved H14 residue, located next to the nucleotide-binding site, is important for enzyme function.
source: This demonstrated that this highly conserved residue, located next to the nucleotide-binding site, is important for enzyme function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of activity in the H14A mutant.

claim: The substitution of the conserved residue E114 had no effect on the activity of Agl24.
source: By contrast, the substitution of the conserved residue E114, opposite of the nucleotide-binding site, had no effect on the activity of Agl24 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by activity assays shown in the figure.

claim: A Km value for acceptor-2 could not be determined using the HPLC system, due to significant substrate inhibition above 0.5 mM.
source: A Km value for acceptor-2 could not be determined using this system, due to significant substrate inhibition above 0.5 mM, however, a Km(app) for UDP-GlcNAc was determined: (UDP-GlcNAc)Km = 1.37 ± 0.13 mM, Vmax = 32.5 ± 0.9 pmol min–1.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis using HPLC.

claim: A Km(app) for UDP-GlcNAc was determined: (UDP-GlcNAc)Km = 1.37 ± 0.13 mM, Vmax = 32.5 ± 0.9 pmol min–1.
source: A Km value for acceptor-2 could not be determined using this system, due to significant substrate inhibition above 0.5 mM, however, a Km(app) for UDP-GlcNAc was determined: (UDP-GlcNAc)Km = 1.37 ± 0.13 mM, Vmax = 32.5 ± 0.9 pmol min–1.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis using HPLC.

claim: The Km values of Agl24 agree with the Km values of other GT enzymes, which typically exhibit Km affinities for their respective nucleotide sugars in the high micromolar range, reflecting the estimated intracellular concentrations of the nucleotide sugar.
source: These results agree with the Km values of other GT enzymes, which typically exhibit Km affinities for their respective nucleotide sugars in the high micromolar range, reflecting the estimated intracellular concentrations of the nucleotide sugar (Varki et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a comparison with known properties of other GTs, supported by citation.

claim: 1H NMR analysis confirmed that the enzymatic product contained two GlcNAc residues with different linkage types based on the presence of two differently coupled anomeric protons.
source: A 1H NMR analysis confirmed that the enzymatic product contained two GlcNAc residues with different linkage types based on the presence of two differently coupled anomeric protons (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in the figures.

claim: One anomeric proton appeared as a doublet of doublets (5.35 ppm, JH1-H2 = 3.1 Hz, JH1-P = 7.2 Hz), typical of an α-linked GlcNAc residue.
source: One anomeric proton appeared as a doublet of doublets (5.35 ppm, JH1-H2 = 3.1 Hz, JH1-P = 7.2 Hz), typical of an α-linked GlcNAc residue (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on NMR analysis and interpretation of coupling constants.

claim: Another anomeric signal appeared as a doublet with a large J coupling value (4.49 ppm, JH1-H2 = 8.5 Hz), indicative of a β-linked GlcNAc residue.
source: Another anomeric signal appeared as a doublet with a large J coupling value (4.49 ppm, JH1-H2 = 8.5 Hz), indicative of a β-linked GlcNAc residue.
evidence: This is based on NMR analysis and interpretation of coupling constants.

claim: The substrate acceptor-2 contained an α-linked GlcNAc; this strongly suggested the terminal GlcNAc introduced by Agl24 was β-linked.
source: The substrate acceptor-2 contained an α-linked GlcNAc; this strongly suggested the terminal GlcNAc introduced by Agl24 was β-linked.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure of the acceptor and NMR data of the product.

claim: The C4 signal of the α-GlcNAc residue was shifted to 79.6 ppm, strongly suggesting that the terminal β-GlcNAc was linked at this position.
source: The C4 signal of the α-GlcNAc residue was shifted to 79.6 ppm, strongly suggesting that the terminal β-GlcNAc was linked at this position.
evidence: This is based on NMR analysis and interpretation of chemical shifts.

source: In conclusion, a combination of 1H NMR and 1D and 2D TOCSY, COSY, and HSQC experiments confirmed that Agl24 is an inverting β-1,4-GlcNAc transferase.
evidence: This is supported by comprehensive NMR analysis.

claim: Agl24-like homologs form a clade containing Crenarchaeota, Bathyarchaeota, and one Baldrarchaeota (Asgard).
source: Agl24-like homologs form a clade containing Crenarchaeota, Bathyarchaeota, and one Baldrarchaeota (Asgard).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

source: These Agl24-like sequences are found in all Crenarchaeota genomes from the orders Fervidicoccales, Acidilobales, Desulfurococcales, and Sulfolobales, but not in members of the order Thermoproteales (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 5, and doi.org/10.7910/DVN/9KSWQR).
evidence: This is based on database searches and phylogenetic analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The Bathyarchaeota (14 sequences, mainly from Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) order o__B26-1) form a strongly supported monophyletic branch within Crenarchaeota resulting from a single lateral transfer event.
source: The Bathyarchaeota (14 sequences, mainly from Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) order o__B26-1) form a strongly supported monophyletic branch within Crenarchaeota (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2) resulting from a single lateral transfer event.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The sister clade of Agl24 consists of the eukaryotic Alg13 and Alg14, as well as EpsF-like and EpsE-like sequences from Archaea and Bacteria.
source: The sister clade of Agl24 consists of the eukaryotic Alg13 and Alg14, as well as EpsF-like and EpsE-like sequences from Archaea and Bacteria.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: With the exception of Perkinsela sp. in Alg13/EpsF, Eukaryotes are monophyletic and form a strongly supported monophyletic branch with an Asgard lineage, Thorarchaeota for Alg13 and Odinarchaeota for Alg14.
source: With the exception of Perkinsela sp. in Alg13/EpsF, Eukaryotes are monophyletic and form a strongly supported monophyletic branch with an Asgard lineage, Thorarchaeota for Alg13 and Odinarchaeota for Alg14.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Other closely related archaeal sequences to Alg13/14 are mainly from Verstraetearchaeota.
source: Other closely related archaeal sequences are mainly from Verstraetearchaeota.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The EpsE/EpsF archaeal sequences (mainly from Euryarchaeota and DPANN) are interspersed with bacterial homologs indicating multiple interdomain transfers.
source: These, along with the EpsE/EpsF archaeal sequences (mainly from Euryarchaeota and DPANN) are interspersed with bacterial homologs indicating multiple interdomain transfers.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The function of EpsE and EpsF has been studied in Lactobacillales, where these enzymes are involved in exopolysaccharide production.
source: The function of EpsE and EpsF has been studied in Lactobacillales, where these enzymes are involved in exopolysaccharide production (Kolkman et al., 1997; De Vuyst et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Similar to Alg14-13, the combined activity of EpsE and EpsF links either a glucose (Glc) from UDP-Glc or a galactose (Gal) from UDP-Gal via a β-1,4 linkage to lipid-linked glucose acceptors, creating either a lipid-linked cellobiose or a lactose, respectively.
source: Similar to Alg14-13, the combined activity of EpsE and EpsF links either a glucose (Glc) from UDP-Glc (Kleerebezem et al., 1999, van Kranenburg et al., 1999), or a galactose (Gal) from UDP-Gal via a β-1,4 linkage to lipid-linked glucose acceptors (van Kranenburg et al., 1999), creating either a lipid-linked cellobiose or a lactose, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: As opposed to Agl24 and the other exclusively archaeal clades in the phylogeny, most EpsE/EpsF and Alg14/Alg13-related genes are split.
source: As opposed to Agl24 and the other exclusively archaeal clades in our phylogeny, most EpsE/EpsF and Alg14/Alg13-related genes are split.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: The split of EpsE/EpsF and Alg14/Alg13-related genes indicates a single gene split event at the base of that clade, followed by multiple independent re-fusion events across Bacteria, Archaea (e.g., some Thorarchaeota), and Eukaryotes (Kinetoplastids, Amoebozoa; in the latter with gene order inversion).
source: This indicates a single gene split event at the base of that clade, followed by multiple independent re-fusion events across Bacteria, Archaea (e.g., some Thorarchaeota), and Eukaryotes (Kinetoplastids, Amoebozoa; in the latter with gene order inversion).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic and genomic analysis.

claim: All other Alg14-13 homolog sequences are exclusively archaeal, fused, and form primarily two clades.
source: All other sequences are exclusively archaeal, fused, and form primarily two clades.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: One clade of Alg14-13 homologs consists mainly of euryarchaeal methanogens and a couple of DPANN.
source: One clade consists mainly of euryarchaeal methanogens and a couple of DPANN.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The distribution of Alg14-13 homologs in certain lineages (Methanococcales, Methanosarcinales) is wide enough to suggest that their respective ancestors possessed an Alg14-13 homolog.
source: The distribution in certain lineages (Methanococcales, Methanosarcinales) is wide enough to suggest that their respective ancestors possessed an Alg14-13 homolog.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution.

claim: The second clade of Alg14-13 homologs corresponds to the TACK superphylum (Thaumarchaeota, Bathyarchaeota, Aigarchaeota, Marsarchaeota, Geothermarchaeota, Nezhaarchaeota, Verstraetearchaeota, and Korarchaeota).
source: The second clade corresponds to the TACK superphylum (Thaum-, Bathy-, Aig-, Mars-, Geotherm-, Nezha-, Verstraete-, and Korarchaeota).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: An Alg14-13 homolog was most probably present at the ancestor of the TACK supergroup.
source: Even though the relationships among lineages are unresolved, an Alg14-13 homolog was most probably present at the ancestor of the TACK supergroup.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution.

claim: Among the TACK, there exist sequences from various Asgard lineages that have been acquired from ancient lateral transfers.
source: Among the TACK, there exist sequences from various Asgard lineages that have been acquired from ancient lateral transfers.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

source: A third clade consisting of divergent Thaumarchaeota sequences is either sister to both TACK and Euryarchaeota-DPANN (Alg13/EpsF, Figure 7A) or only the TACK.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Divergent homologs of Alg14-13 exist across multiple archaeal lineages, including one in Bathyarchaeota (mainly in GTDB genus g__PALSA-986) and two in Methanobacteriales.
source: Although we used only well-established Alg14-13 homologs from Lombard, 2016, in our phylogenies, such divergent homologs (often forming distinct clades) exist across multiple archaeal lineages, including one in Bathyarchaeota (mainly in GTDB genus g__PALSA-986) and two in Methanobacteriales (doi.org/10.7910/DVN/9KSWQR).
evidence: This is based on database searches and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Some of the Bathyarchaeota and the GTDB o__Thermofilales (NCBI: unclassified Thermoprotei) member B67-G16 in the TACK clade additionally possess an Agl24.
source: Some of the Bathyarchaeota and the GTDB o__Thermofilales (NCBI: unclassified Thermoprotei) member B67-G16 in the TACK clade above additionally possess an Agl24.
evidence: This is based on database searches and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Some Bathyarchaeota MAGs also contain additional sequences from the unused divergent clades.
source: Some Bathyarchaeota MAGs also contain additional sequences from the unused divergent clades (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and doi.org/10.7910/DVN/9KSWQR).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Since the N-glycosylation processes of Bathyarchaeota are unknown, it is impossible to predict the function and overlap of these homologs.
source: Since their N-glycosylation processes are unknown, it is impossible to predict the function and overlap thereof of these homologs.
evidence: This represents a limitation in interpreting the genomic data.

source: Outgroup-free rooting with the minimal ancestor deviation (MAD) method (Tria et al., 2017) corroborates the outgroup rooting of the phylogenies with MurG (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis using different rooting methods.

claim: The bacterial MurG and various (primarily) archaeal Agl24/Alg14-13/EpsEF homologs seem to have originated from a split at the Last Universal Common Ancestor, as previously proposed.
source: The bacterial MurG and various (primarily) archaeal Agl24/Alg14-13/EpsEF homologs seem to have originated from a split at the Last Universal Common Ancestor, as previously proposed (Lombard, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis, supported by citation to a previous proposal.

source: Although EpsE/EpsF and Alg14/Alg13-like sequences are found in Bacteria which are ancient in some lineages (EpsE/EpsF in Actinobacteria and Cyanobacteria, see the preliminary phylogenies in doi.org/10.7910/DVN/9KSWQR), these homologs are of archaeal origin and were acquired through ancient interdomain transfers.

claim: The eukaryotic branches of Alg14/13 are internally poorly resolved and do not even recover the major clades of that domain, such as Opisthokonts.
source: Similarly, the respective eukaryotic branches are internally poorly resolved and do not even recover the major clades of that domain, such as Opisthokonts.

source: We cannot reveal if this is purely due to weak phylogenetic signal or horizontal gene transfer events, however, the eukaryotic Alg14-13 are monophyletic and archaeal in origin.
evidence: This represents a limitation of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The eukaryotic Alg14-13 are monophyletic and archaeal in origin.
source: We cannot reveal if this is purely due to weak phylogenetic signal or horizontal gene transfer events, however, the eukaryotic Alg14-13 are monophyletic and archaeal in origin.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: One possibility is that Alg14-13 were present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA), as proposed in Lombard, 2016.
source: One possibility is that they were present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA), as proposed in Lombard, 2016.

source: The proximity of Asgards to Eykaryotes would suggest that these genes were inherited vertically during eukaryogenesis in a two-domain tree of life (Eme et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on phylogenetic proximity, supported by citations.

source: The counterargument is that only two Asgard phyla are in the vicinity of Eukaryotes, and neither is Heimdallarchaeota, as would be expected from the literature.

source: Despite our careful analysis, we did not find Alg13- and Alg14-like sequences in most Asgard species, suggesting that if they produce the same type of glycosylation, they could be using a different enzyme for this step of N-glycosylation.
evidence: This is based on database searches and represents a speculation about alternative enzymes.

source: The homologs in Wukong-, Baldr-, Borrarchaeota, DTBI01, and a second homolog in Odinarchaeota have been laterally acquired from within the TACK.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: It is unknown whether the multiple Odinarchaeota genes have overlapping functions.
source: It is unknown whether the multiple Odinarchaeota genes have overlapping functions.
evidence: This represents a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The alternative scenario to eukaryogenesis involves a very ancient interdomain transfer from Archaea to either proto-Eukaryotes or shortly after the LECA.
source: The alternative scenario to eukaryogenesis involves a very ancient interdomain transfer from Archaea to either proto-Eukaryotes or shortly after the LECA.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis for the origin of eukaryotic Alg14-13.

claim: The history of Alg14-13 involving a very ancient interdomain transfer is compatible with both a two- and three-domain tree of life.
source: Even if such a history is compatible with both a two- and three-domain tree of life, our phylogenies do not directly support a three-domain tree.
evidence: This is a statement about the compatibility of the hypothesis with different tree topologies.

claim: The phylogenies do not directly support a three-domain tree.
source: Even if such a history is compatible with both a two- and three-domain tree of life, our phylogenies do not directly support a three-domain tree.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

source: Whether with MurG outgroup rooting or MAD outgroup-free rooting, the Eukaryotes emerge from and are not sister to all Archaea.
